subtitle: Folding a relative clause into a describing word, and what endings give away
words.intro: A letter from the tax office has its own German. Whole subordinate clauses are folded up in front of a noun, and you only get to the noun at the end. Then you find out you owe 14 euros.

document.intro: A real preface to a book of model letters, from about 1900. It’s complaining that nobody has time and everything has become complicated. Look for a phrase folded in front of a noun, and a je … desto.
document.fact: Fraktur was still the normal German type when this was printed. The writer complains of a *ungeheure Entwickelung*, a monstrous growth, of paperwork. He would enjoy the present.

reading.intro: Maya has received her first real letter from the tax office. She has read it three times. Now she brings it to Frau Huber’s kitchen, together with a cake, because Frau Huber’s late husband worked in that office for forty years, and she’s the only person who can translate.
reading.photos[0].caption: Auch ein Amt: Innen liegen die in vierzig Jahren gesammelten Akten.
reading.photos[1].caption: Ein gelbes Amt mit einem kleinen Dach, unter dem niemand warten möchte.
reading.fact: Many German employees don’t have to file a tax return, but those who do often get around 1,000 euros back. So every year, millions fill in *die Steuererklärung*, by now mostly online, through a system called ELSTER.
